title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
summary: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
story_key: model:claude|title:how the claude code team thinks about verification
content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to fool–either the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concrete

title: Keep the Process, Change the Supplier: Runtime Governance for Tool-Using AI Agents
summary: Tool-using AI agents propose actions whose authorization and external effects cannot be inferred from generated text alone. We study an execution boundary that separates agent proposals from business-controlled authority, context disclosure, and supplier selection. The Open Process Control Plane (OPCP) mediates capability calls and records uncertain outcomes when a supplier may have acted without returning an acceptable reply. We evaluate this runtime with scripted requests and synthetic suppliers: 2,400 fault episodes across four policies, 60 process-termination/restart episodes, 19,000 timed calls across 19 configurations, five targeted mutations over 43 fixtures, and 160 substitution records. No language model or autonomous agent is evaluated. OPCP and a conservative composition agree on all measured fault outcomes. Both recover after definite refusal without cross-supplier duplication; retry-all duplicates effects in every tested lost-reply-after-commit case. Persistent runtime state prevents cross-supplier replay in the restart experiments, while same-supplier duplicate prevention also requires supplier idempotency. At 128 suppliers, best-score routing has a median latency of 1.411 ms versus 0.261 ms for pinned routing. All five selected mutations are detected, and record enumeration exposes acceptance of an empty regression set. These results characterize an execution mechanism relevant to agent governance, including its costs and assumption boundaries. They do not establish improved agent task success, prompt-injection resistance, or real-vendor model portability.

title: TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
summary: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU--GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20--59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40--3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.

title: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency
story_key: story|ver:27|title:daisyrose 27b pushing the frontier of post training efficiency
content_excerpt: Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B , RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles . We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0% . Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks. The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window . The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings. We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats. After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000 , you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client: The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content , and its final answer in content . These settings follow the model card’s quickstart . DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%. Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings. Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes. We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI , starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set. RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. title: Your Software Factory Needs a Bill of Materials | Daniel Meppiel
summary:
Developers are about to write skills instead of code, and Microsoft's Daniel Meppiel argues the software factory that runs them needs versioning, a bill of materials and signed receipts before enterprises will trust it.

Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks:
https://tessl.co/7jw

Recorded live at AI DevCon NYC 2026, Simon Maple sits down with Daniel, of Microsoft's Global Black Belt team and creator of APM (Agent Package Manager), to dig into why teams keep rebuilding the same skills, how to version a skill when the change is in its behavior rather than a method signature, and why skills can only ever be guidance while security controls stay deterministic. Then stay for Daniel's full DevCon talk, Version Your Factory, Not Just Your Code, on agent contracts, signed receipts and the evidence a regulated enterprise needs before it auto-merges.

What we cover:
– Why developers will write skills and prose instead of code
– Why teams keep rebuilding the same skills, and the case for a shared skill catalog
– Testing and versioning skills with evals: when is a change a major version?
– APM, lock files and an agent bill of materials for your software factory
– Skills are guidance, security controls are deterministic
– Daniel's AI DevCon talk: agent contracts, signed receipts and auto-merging on evidence

title: How Public Evals Work and Fail, and What Should Change
summary: How to read eval scores and what to question, from a teardown of 12 benchmarks.
story_key: story|title:how public evals work and fail and what should change
content_excerpt: As models ship faster, eval scores are often the first thing we learn about a new model. But how much weight should we put in them? In eight of twelve public evals studied, there’s evidence the grader failed work that should have passed. And even when the grader gets it right, many benchmarks measure what’s easy rather than what matters, and should instead focus on reliability, work velocity, multi-turn collaboration, etc. Here, we’ll cover the common patterns and principles, the errors models make, and where current benchmarks fall short. I’ll also share what we’re getting wrong and what should change, including why average pass rate isn’t enough and why dollars are the wrong measure of cost. Finally, we’ll walk through twelve evals: four on coding and science, six on knowledge work, and two on browsing and computer use. By the end, you’ll know what to trust in a benchmark and what to question. In addition, eval benchmarks are increasingly maintained like software. They ship versioned releases and accept fixes through issues and pull requests. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 retired 30 tasks and revised 57 others, and Harvey LAB’s public set has grown from about 1,250 tasks to 2,010 since launching in May 2026. Like software, these releases can also introduce breaking changes—Terminal Bench can drop saturated tasks with each version, making scores hard to compare across releases. Deterministic checks over LLM judges. Code-based checks are reproducible and won’t shift rankings when a judge model is updated. DeepSWE and AutomationBench avoid LLM judges altogether, and Agents’ Last Exam goes to great lengths to minimize them. When an eval does need a judge—for a legal memo or clinical response—it narrows the judge’s job to binary yes/no rubric items rather than a holistic score. Graders check the outcome, not the steps. The intent is to allow any approach that produces the right result to pass. For example, Terminal Bench inspects the final state of the container and ignores the agent’s intermediate commands or console output. AutomationBench, OSWorld 2.0, and DeepSWE work the same way. All-pass scoring is common because partial work often isn’t usable. Under all-pass scoring, a task passes only if every test or criterion passes. DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, Terminal Bench Science, AutomationBench, and Harvey LAB score this way. As Harvey puts it, “there is no partial credit for catching most of the issues”—a report that flags eight of ten risks is incomplete, not 80% us

title: LangSmith for Coding Agents: Now track spend by outcome
summary: LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce.
story_key: story|title:langsmith for coding agents now track spend by outcome
content_excerpt: Coding is the largest category of enterprise AI application spend, reaching $34B in 2026 . Every company now wants to know what all that spend returns, but most engineering leaders still can’t give an exact answer to what it's buying. To try to understand coding agent ROI, teams used to look at high-level data like usage analytics and AI consumption, but these don’t provide insight into what tokens actually produce. Answering the ROI question is hard and requires visibility into spend across users and teams, along with a way to connect it to outcomes. We felt this friction firsthand when spend with our own coding agent, Robin, started climbing, and is one of the reasons we built a model router. Now we're excited to offer a practical solution for our customers too. LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce. This provides a clearer way to calculate the ROI behind coding agent budgets and understand how changes to models and policies impact it. The new LangSmith Agent Platform operates around the agent. Each agent has its own record and belongs to an "agent type" that determines what its dashboard shows, which data it connects to, and how it's evaluated. Coding agents are the first specialized agent type, and present data on pull requests, one of the signs that the agent's work is useful. LangSmith already traces coding agents across model providers, including Claude Code and Codex . With coding agents in LangSmith, the spend in each trace is automatically attributed to pull requests each agent contributed to. The attribution reflects the tasks a coding agent is used for. It covers both cases where a single thread can open several PRs, and where a PR can take several threads to finish, so data in LangSmith reflects what your agents actually accomplished and what it cost. Up until today, LangSmith enabled you to see the cost per trace for any of your coding agents, one trace at a time. This is useful for manual debugging, but doesn't provide visibility into trends across the entire team. The new coding agent overview page aggregates those costs and ties them to the pull requests your agents worked on. The dashboard shows KPIs at a glance, and clicking any metric opens its trend over time. For example, if your team switched models, you can compare before and after to see the impact of the change. title: Genie 4 is now available

We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
summary: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.

title: Kaer: Security-Aware Replanning for Multi-Agent Systems
summary:
One popular architecture for multi-agent systems (MAS) relies on an orchestrator that generates an initial plan, coordinates its execution, and dynamically revises the plan based on agent feedback when tasks cannot be fully specified in advance. This dynamic replanning introduces a critical vulnerability: malicious agents can embed instructions within their feedback to hijack the replanning process. Existing defenses focus exclusively on per-tool access control or static, pre-execution policy enforcement, leaving the replanning phase unsecured.
  We introduce Kaer, a multi-agent framework featuring security-aware replanning. Kaer shields the planner from untrusted agent feedback by conveying diagnostics to the replanning procedure strictly through abstract templates. Plan revisions are restricted to a set of deterministic repair operators, and all modified plans must satisfy preset policies. We create Cintra, a benchmark of simulated user tasks requiring replanning paired with adversarial objectives targeting the replanning phase. Using Cintra, we evaluate both task completion rates and system vulnerability to replanning exploits by malicious agents. Evaluating Kaer on Cintra against Magentic-One (an undefended MAS) and ControlValve (the state-of-the-art defense) demonstrates that Kaer achieves higher robustness than both systems while maintaining comparable utility to ControlValve. Although abstract failure templates slightly constrain utility on select tasks, Kaer enables MAS to perform secure, dynamic plan revisions without exposing the orchestrator to untrusted agent feedback.

  • Added an esc to stop footer hint in a subagent's view where Esc would stop it

  • Added overflowX="scroll" on a mod's Box, and maxLines and wrap="clip" on its Text
  • Fixed cp of a file being refused when only its source was covered by an Edit deny rule
  • Fixed Bash commands that delete or overwrite files (find -delete, cat a > b, sort -o) being summed up in the transcript as a search or a read
  • Fixed a misleading "Dangerous rm operation" warning in the Bash permission prompt on some commands with no rm that Claude Code can't read reliably
  • Fixed background sessions losing the LLM gateway your shell exported after a crash, after a reopen from another folder, or when the background service lacks it: they now stop before any model request
  • Fixed the background service ending your own processes, such as an SSH login, when a process number on its list had been reused by another user's process
  • Fixed rules added in /permissions or at a main-conversation tool prompt, and /add-dir folders, looking saved when the settings file couldn't be written; the terminal now warns and names it
  • Fixed a failed MCP headersHelper, or one not run in an untrusted folder, making other sessions start without that server, for most servers with no stored OAuth refresh token
  • Fixed managed settings with certain key names stopping Claude Code from starting or affecting other managed files
  • Fixed settings files with values nested thousands of levels deep crashing Claude Code or applying only some of the time; values past 64 levels are now dropped with a warning
  • Fixed a settings file saved with an error mid-session being skipped silently; a warning now names the file
  • Fixed the subagent model set in managed settings not applying in Claude Desktop's Code tab; it now overrides your own, as in a terminal, unless those settings also pick a provider or gateway
  • Fixed sandboxed commands failing to start on Linux when the home or config directory is reached through a symlink into /net and sandbox settings deny reads of it
  • Fixed empty placeholder files, including .git/config.lock, sometimes being left in the project on Linux when Claude Code was stopped during a sandboxed command
  • Fixed Up then Enter answering Yes at the folder trust prompt shown under an already trusted parent folder
  • Fixed an extra Enter at the end of setup accepting the offer to make auto mode the default
  • Fixed a message typed over the startup auto mode offer being lost, and its Enter accepting the offer
  • Fixed a note typed on a permission prompt being sent to Claude after Tab had hidden it
  • Fixed PreToolUse hooks in managed settings leaving no OpenTelemetry tool_decision event or permission_denials entry when they refused a direct tool call
  • Fixed letters typed over /sandbox or a delete question in /permissions moving the selection

  • Changed the Bash sandbox to keep its state in some cases during a session, until you run /sandbox or /cd; Bash may ask first
  • Changed sandboxed commands on macOS, Linux and WSL to no longer write to some sensitive home folders by default; some can be allowed with sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite in user or managed settings
  • Changed the Bash sandbox to set aside unexpected entries in a repository's .git folder after a command
  • Changed the Bash sandbox on Linux and WSL to create some missing --add-dir folders before each sandboxed command, so commands that create them can fail, skip, or land inside them
  • Changed commands that a permission hook or SDK host rewrites while approving to stay in the sandbox if the original was checked as sandboxed; the approver can add dangerouslyDisableSandbox: true
  • Changed claude mcp serve to ignore sandbox.excludedCommands
  • Changed /rewind on macOS, Linux and WSL to leave some files untouched and report them as skipped when the sandbox is on
  • Changed the Bash sandbox to ask before some lines that set environment variables when auto-allow is off; unattended runs can refuse them
  • Changed Claude's file tools to refuse writes to Claude Code's sign-in files, such as .credentials.json
  • Changed the Bash permission check to ask before more commands reach Claude Code's sign-in files
  • Changed some file tools to refuse some device and process files
  • Changed some cp and mv commands to ask first
  • Changed some tool calls in bypass permissions mode to ask for approval, or be denied where no one can be asked
  • Changed the Bash permission check to ask about some commands with very long values it can't finish checking, or to refuse them where a deny rule may apply or no one can answer
  • Changed subagents isolated in a worktree to refuse, in any repository, some git commands in Bash that can rewrite branches shared with your checkout; sessions are not affected
  • Changed ExitWorktree to refuse removing a worktree while a background subagent or shell command may still be running in it, unless Claude passes discard_changes
  • Changed the computer use macOS permissions panel to ignore j and k; the arrow keys and Ctrl+P/Ctrl+N still move the selection
  • Changed the PowerShell tool to ask before some more commands; unattended runs refuse them unless an allow rule, auto mode or bypass permissions mode allows them
  • Changed the PowerShell tool to ask about some more commands, even in bypass permissions mode, and to refuse some of them
  • Changed some malformed PowerShell commands to be denied
  • Changed some PowerShell tool commands that define a function named like a built-in command to be refused, so Claude can rename it
  • Changed auto mode to ignore some wildcard shell allow rules, such as ones that name no program or that start with $HOME, so the safety check decides those commands
  • Changed auto mode to judge wildcard allow rules whose program is a Windows backslash path, so those calls can be blocked; exact rules keep their allow; we plan to restore rules that start with .\
  • Changed a managed autoMode.environment list without "$defaults" to replace every built-in entry in Claude Desktop and Agent SDK apps too; add "$defaults" or copy the sensitive-target ones
  • Changed --add-dir and /add-dir in local terminal sessions to show the trust prompt for a folder you have not trusted yet; claude --bg refuses such a folder
  • Changed self-hosted runners under --trust-workspace false to ignore more repository settings; set such values in user or managed settings
  • Changed how permission answers over Remote Control and on self-hosted runners save "always allow" choices
  • Changed enabled plugins that were refused for a malformed plugin.json display field: they now load, with their hooks and MCP servers; administrators should check the plugins they deploy
  • Changed how allowedHttpHookUrls and httpHookAllowedEnvVars apply to hooks from managed settings
  • Changed HTTP hooks to ignore Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding in their headers setting; the request's length comes from its body
  • Changed plugin uninstall to also delete the files extracted from the plugin's MCP bundles (.mcpb, .dxt), unless another plugin uses the same bundle
  • Changed some worktree sessions to skip some plugin settings; a notice names what was skipped
  • Changed /plugin uninstall, remove and switch questions to lists answered with the arrow keys and Enter, or Esc to cancel; y, n and u no longer answer them
  • Changed automatic compaction in plan mode to use the model answering you, such as Opus with opusplan, so it can cost more
  • Changed Cowork cloud sessions to hold an organization's OpenTelemetry export until the first turn; a session that gets no message now sends nothing, so claude_code.session.count can fall
  • Changed Claude's messages to a session on another machine to be refused when your session uses an API key, auth token, profile or workload identity beside a saved claude.ai login
  • Changed --bare sessions on an unapproved API key: moving one to the background is now refused in most setups, and claude --bare --bg exits with an error if the background service lacks the key
  • Changed "Continue automatically at usage limit" to stop with a notice, sending nothing, when your login changes or ends during the wait
  • Remote Control: Changed how it connects through a proxy: requests now use a CONNECT tunnel, so a proxy that refuses CONNECT stops Remote Control with an error
  • Remote Control: Changed the session debug logs written under --verbose to go to ~/.claude/child-logs/
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed Linux and macOS sessions with no gh to get a built-in gh api by default, via Anthropic, which adds their GitHub sign-in, if any; --use-anthropic-gh false turns it off
  • Changed agent view so that quitting with Ctrl+C twice, Ctrl+D twice or /exit after pressing ← in an empty conversation ends that session, instead of leaving it running for 5 minutes
  • Changed --await-initialize to be refused with --bg or --worktree --tmux, which never read the initialize request, instead of starting without the fields it carries
  • Changed worktree creation, /teleport and IDE checkouts to run git with a stricter PATH; a git filter or helper may need its full path
  • Changed the card for approving a subagent's plan to two choices, "Yes, and switch to default (ask each time) for this session" and "No", chosen with the arrow keys and Enter (typed text moves to No)
  • Changed the /claude-api skill to build agents on Managed Agents by default, unless you want to host the agent loop yourself
  • Changed /usage in fullscreen mode to show plan limit bars before session cost for subscribers; /cost still starts with cost
  • Changed the wording of some messages that claude subcommands print; JSON output is unchanged
  • Changed first-run setup to preselect the "Auto (match terminal)" theme instead of Dark mode
  • Changed fullscreen /cd to refuse "Yes" while its trust prompt doesn't fit, with a line saying to make the window taller
  • Removed the tmux notice that said the mouse wheel needs set -g mouse on in fullscreen; the wheel scrolls without it
  • Removed the spinner tip that suggested /clear 30 minutes into a running turn
  • [VSCode] Added a claudeCode.promptSuggestions setting that turns prompt suggestions off
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Rewind code to here" in a forked conversation sometimes undoing one turn too many and deleting files created in that turn
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Sandbox dialog creating empty files and folders in the home directory and the project's .git folder while the sandbox is off
  • [VSCode] Fixed the saved sign-in being lost on some networks
  • [VSCode] Fixed sign-in ending when a verification code, a web address or a code from another sign-in attempt is pasted; the panel now says what to paste instead
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen showing briefly each time a panel or window opened while signed in to Console without an API key
  • [VSCode] Fixed the usage-limit banner's "Request more" button for Team and Enterprise members coming back after each press without sending anything, after you signed in again during a session
  • [VSCode] Fixed /ide in a second Claude Code session silently losing the editor connection back to the first session; the newest connection now wins and the displaced session shows how to switch back
  • [VSCode] Fixed saved memories not being listed in the Memory dialog, or RAM use growing without end, when the memory folder held symlink loops, and a hang when it held a named pipe
  • [VSCode] Fixed a running command's live output stopping after one failed read
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Open in Terminal" showing only the shell's error when claude could not be started: in bash, zsh, fish and Git Bash, a notice now explains why and links to the install guide
  • [VSCode] Fixed the panel showing no "Open artifact" link after Claude publishes an artifact
  • [VSCode] Fixed the prompt suggestion hiding the "attach selected text" hint while the chat panel is unfocused
  • [VSCode] Fixed buttons with no visible border in the high-contrast themes, and the dark welcome art on the sign-in screen in Light High Contrast
  • [VSCode] Improved Edit and Write speed: no wait for new problems on files that are not open in a tab when the editor has been reporting none for such files
  • [VSCode] Changed a running command's live output in the chat to look like the command card's OUT row
  • [VSCode] Changed the text of extension errors in event listeners, views and activation to stay out of the editor's own error telemetry
